prompt.context: A diversified manufacturing client has asked a consulting firm to help turn around its steam boiler hose division. The division supplies boiler hoses to both external customers and to the client's own boiler division. Key industry context: boiler hoses are sold both with original equipment and as replacements; there has been increasing price pressure in the industry; the client is third of eight industry participants.
prompt.question: How would you structure an analysis aimed at restoring profitability? Where do you expect to save costs?

clarifying_info.q: What does the P&L look like?
clarifying_info.a: Last year P&L (as a percent of sales): Raw material 70%, Labor 20%, Distributed overhead 10%, SG&A 15%, Profit (15%).

clarifying_info.q: What type of raw material is used?
clarifying_info.a: Raw material is a commodity petrochemical.
At least two of the other eight companies in the industry are making moderate profits.

clarifying_info.q: Can the client simply exit the product line?
clarifying_info.a: Dropping the product line is apparently not possible because hoses are necessary for boiler sales.

framework: Assess whether to exit the business (dropped — hoses required for boiler sales)
Benchmark raw material costs vs. competitors (commodity petrochemical — same price for all)
Review overhead allocation methodology (limited savings potential)
Examine SG&A costs (standard industry fee paid for independent installers)
Investigate scale economies and production technology
Analyze labor costs (wage rate and productivity)
Investigate product design / engineering specifications vs. market requirements
Explore organizational linkage between engineering and marketing/sales

questions.prompt: Raw material is 70% of sales yet is a commodity petrochemical. What purchasing practices might explain a cost disadvantage?
questions.guidance: The candidate should explore whether contracts are structured favorably. The answer: materials are purchased through long-term contracts priced at list minus a discount — same as industry. This rules out purchasing as the root cause.

questions.prompt: Labor is 20% of sales. Is that a source of the problem?
questions.guidance: Candidate should benchmark wage rate and productivity against industry. Answer: both are average for the industry. Labor is not the root cause.

questions.prompt: The client is the third-largest of eight players and has a modern plant. Could scale or technology explain the cost gap?
questions.guidance: Neither scale nor technology is the root cause — the client is large enough for scale economies and has a modern plant.

questions.prompt: Given that raw material, labor, scale, and technology all appear competitive, where is the excess cost coming from?
questions.guidance: The best answer arrives at over-engineering: the product has been over-designed, requiring excess raw material. Because raw material is 70% of sales, even modest over-design creates a large cost penalty. Candidates should connect the insight to organizational root causes: little contact between engineering and marketing/sales means the product is engineered to exceed what customers actually require.

brainstorming.prompt: What organizational implications follow from the finding that the product is over-designed?

categories.name: Engineering–Market Linkage
ideas: Assess how the product engineering operation is connected to the marketplace
There is currently little contact between engineering and marketing/sales organizations
Restructure communication channels so engineering receives regular market input

categories.name: Customer & Sales Feedback
ideas: Determine what feedback the sales force is receiving from customers
Customers are delighted with the hoses but do not require all the product features
Use voice-of-customer data to right-size specifications

categories.name: Broader Organizational Audit
ideas: Identify other areas in the company where similar over-design problems may exist
Conduct a cross-divisional review of product specifications vs. customer requirements

recommendation: Reduce raw material content by redesigning the boiler hose to match actual customer requirements rather than exceeding them; this directly attacks the 70% raw-material cost base
Fix the organizational disconnect between engineering and marketing/sales so product specifications are continuously calibrated to market needs
risks: Over-simplified design could compromise product quality or reliability if done without rigorous testing
Sales force and customers who prize the current quality must be carefully managed through the transition
Similar over-design issues likely exist in other divisions, creating a broader change-management challenge
next_steps: Map current hose specifications against customer requirements to quantify over-design and target material savings
Pilot a redesigned hose with select customers to validate performance at reduced specification
Establish regular engineering–sales–marketing reviews to prevent recurrence
Conduct a company-wide audit for analogous over-design issues in other product lines
